title: Deduction Detective
intro: Must be, might be, can't be — reading the clues to deduce, not just guess. How certain are you, really?

A2.right: I'm sure, because the clues tell me so — a deduction
A2.why: Clues make you sure: “He has a sheriff’s star. He must be the sheriff.”

A2.right: I'm almost certain it's not true — strong negative deduction
A2.why: The opposite of “must be” is “can’t be”, never “mustn’t be”.

A2.right: it's possible, but I'm not sure — 'might not' means maybe not
A2.why: “Might be” means maybe it is; “might not be” means maybe it isn’t.

A2.right: it's possible — but 'couldn't be' means impossible
A2.why: “Could be” is possible, but “couldn’t be” is a strong no, like “can’t be”.

A2.right: it's possible, a little formal — two words, not 'maybe'
A2.why: “May be” (two words) is the verb; “maybe” (one word) means “quizás”.
“Probably” goes after “is”: “He is probably at home.”

A2.right: a known fact, no doubt at all — no deduction needed
A2.why: “Definitely” is for something you know, not a guess from clues.
“Isn’t likely to be” means probably not; “likely” is followed by “to”.

A2.right: it seems so from what I can see
A2.why: “Looks like” + noun for what you see: “It looks like rain.”

A2.right: it seems so from what I can hear
A2.why: “Sounds like” for what you hear: “That sounds like the stagecoach.”

A2.right: it seems so from the smell
A2.why: “Smells like” for your nose: “It smells like paella in here.”

A2.right: it seems so from touching it
A2.why: “Feels like” for your hands: “This feels like silk.”

B1.right: I'm sure it happened — strong past deduction
B1.why: Must have + past participle: a confident deduction about the past.
The negative of “must have been” is “can’t have been”, never “mustn’t have been”.

B1.right: it's possible it happened, but I'm not sure
B1.why: Might have + past participle: possible in the past, but you can’t be sure.

B1.right: I expect it, if all goes to plan — 'the train should be here soon'
B1.why: “Should be” is what you expect if things go normally.

B1.right: almost certain to happen — 'it's bound to rain'
B1.why: “Bound to” is a near-certain prediction: “It’s bound to be busy during the Fallas.”

B1.right: the evidence or my impression suggests it is — the everyday choice
B1.why: “Seems to be” is soft and common in speech: you report an impression.

B1.right: it looks like it is — more formal, used in reports and the news
B1.why: “Appears to be” is the formal cousin of “seems to be”.

B1.right: probably not, based on the evidence
B1.why: “Unlikely to” means probably not; like “likely”, it takes “to”.

B1.right: I'm sure it's happening right now
B1.why: Must be + -ing: “The light’s on; he must be working.”

B1.right: I'm sure it isn't happening right now
B1.why: Can’t be + -ing: “It’s silent; the machine can’t be working.”

B1.right: it was expected, but it didn't happen
B1.why: Should have + past participle: it was the plan, but it didn’t happen.
Might not have + participle: maybe not; much weaker than “can’t have”.

B2.right: I'm sure the person isn't telling the truth
B2.why: Must be + -ing: “His story keeps changing. He must be lying.”
“Possibly” after “can’t” makes the impossibility even stronger.

B2.right: there's a good chance it's true
B2.why: “Well” after could, may or might raises the chance: quite likely, not just possible.

B2.right: very probable — a high chance, but not certain
B2.why: “Highly likely” means very probable; “highly”, not “very much”, goes with likely.
“Hardly” is almost negative already: very unlikely. Don’t add “not”.

B2.right: I'm confident, and I expect you to agree
B2.why: “Surely” adds feeling: you’re confident and expect the listener to agree.

B2.right: there's a good chance it happened
B2.why: May well have + past participle: a good chance it happened.

B2.right: cannot say for certain that something is false
B2.why: To rule something out is to exclude it; if you can’t, it is still possible.

B2.right: I'm sure that action was in progress at a past moment
B2.why: Must have been + -ing: “He was covered in dust; he must have been riding all day.”

B2.right: I'm sure the person didn't know at the time
B2.why: Can’t have + past participle: “He can’t have known about the robbery.”

B2.right: people say so — reported, not proven
B2.why: Passive reporting: “The old mine is said to be full of gold.”

B2.right: it was due already, so I'm starting to worry
B2.why: Should have + participle + “by now”: it was expected already.

C1.right: it logically follows, based on the facts
C1.why: The conclusion follows from logic: “It stands to reason that dirty water spreads disease.”
A formal “almost certainly”: “In all probability, the patient will recover.”

C1.right: certain enough to be accepted as fact
C1.why: The standard in a criminal trial: so certain that no sensible person doubts it.

C1.right: all the signs agree, with nothing against it
C1.why: “Every indication” means every sign points the same way: a strong, formal deduction.

C1.right: it's true, but so shocking it's hard to believe
C1.why: For true but shocking facts: “It defies belief that surgeons once refused to wash their hands.”

C1.left: one could be forgiven for assuming
C1.right: it would be an understandable, if wrong, conclusion
C1.why: A polite way to say a natural assumption is actually wrong.

C1.right: the result is certain before it even happens
C1.why: The outcome is settled in advance: “The election was a foregone conclusion.”

C1.right: more likely true than not, weighing the evidence
C1.why: The civil-court standard: more likely than not, lower than “beyond reasonable doubt”.

C1.right: it is possible to imagine, even if unlikely
C1.why: “Conceivable” means it can be imagined: possible, but not likely.

C1.right: this seems true, said cautiously and formally
C1.why: A careful, formal deduction: “It would appear that the safe was opened from inside.”

C1.right: it's impossible to know or predict
C1.why: Nobody can know: “There’s no telling what the outlaws will do next.”

C1.right: I'm offering a modest guess, not a firm deduction
C1.why: To hazard a guess is to risk one: a tentative, modest deduction.
